tip: 'Enak di-' = nice to X: 'enak didengar' = nice to listen to; 'enak dimakan' = tasty.
'Di-...-i' often means 'on': 'diduduki' = sat on. 'Kursi yang diduduki tamu' = the chair the guest sits on.
'Pe-' turns a verb into the doer: 'jual' (sell) → 'penjual' (seller).
'Pe-' copies the 'meN-' sound change: 'tulis' → 'menulis', so the writer is 'penulis'.
Indonesian rarely marks plurals, but 'para' does it for people: 'para pekerja' = the workers, as a group. It never goes on things.
'Menyanyi' has no object; when a song is named, use 'menyanyikan': 'menyanyikan lagu daerah'.
One root 'ajar', two people: 'pengajar' is the teacher (from 'mengajar', to teach), 'pelajar' the student (from 'belajar', to study).
One root, two people: 'pelajar' learns, 'pengajar' teaches – both from 'ajar'. The 'pe-' prefix builds 'the person who does X' nouns.
'Pe-' also builds doers from nouns: 'kemudi' is the steering wheel, so 'pengemudi' is the driver – the person at the 'kemudi'.
One root, two nouns: 'pelukis' is the painter, 'lukisan' is the painting.
Compound nouns normally run head first: 'pemandu wisata' is literally 'guide tourism' – the reverse of English 'tour guide'.
A few doer nouns take bare 'pe-' with no sound change: 'tani' gives 'petani' (farmer), not 'penani' – 'kerja' gives 'pekerja' the same way.
The suffix '-an' often names the result: 'makan' (eat) → 'makanan' (food, the thing eaten).
'Bangun' means both 'wake up' and 'build'. 'Bangunan' comes from the second: a thing built, a building.
'Masakan' is the dish, the result of cooking; the act itself is 'masak'/'memasak'.
'Sayur' is a vegetable dish; 'sayuran' with '-an' covers vegetables in general.
Before a verb, 'baru' is not 'new' – it means 'only just / only then': 'baru datang setelah tiga puluh menit' = only came after thirty minutes.
The suffix '-an' usually makes things, but 'kenalan' is a person: someone you know. 'Kenalan lama' = an old acquaintance, not old knowledge.
'Oleh-oleh', souvenirs you bring back, is a fixed doubled word – don't read it as the preposition 'oleh' (by) said twice.
'Pe-…-an' wraps a whole activity into a noun: 'kerja' → 'pekerjaan' (work, a job).
'Jalan' → 'perjalanan': the whole journey, not just the road.
'Per-…-an' nouns pair with 'ber-' verbs: 'bertemu' (meet) gives 'pertemuan' (a meeting), just as 'berjalan' gives 'perjalanan'.
'Inap' (stay over) → 'penginapan': a place to stay the night.
To name an action, take the 'meN-' verb and swap 'me-' for 'pe-', then add '-an': 'memeriksa' (check) becomes 'pemeriksaan' (a check).
Time gets eaten in Indonesian: 'memakan waktu satu jam' = takes an hour, literally 'eats one hour'.
'Penjualan' is the selling, 'penjual' the seller – one '-an' apart. 'Penjualan tiket konser' = concert ticket sales, an activity, not a person.
'Ke-…-an' makes a state noun: 'sehat' (healthy) → 'kesehatan' (health).
'Ke-…-an' also names events, and the verb stays whole inside: 'berangkat' (depart) sits intact in 'keberangkatan' (departure).
'Ke-…-an' can mean 'hit by': 'hujan' (rain) → 'kehujanan' (caught in the rain).
'Kehilangan' takes its object directly: 'kehilangan dompet' = losing the wallet – no word for 'of' in between.
